audioscript.text: Part 1, you will hear a woman called Jan, phoning a man about their local conservation group.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Hello.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: Oh hello, my name is Jan.
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: Are you the right person to talk to about the Buckworth Conservation Group?
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: Yes, I'm Peter, I'm the secretary.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: Good, I've just moved to this area, and I'm interested in getting involved.
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: I was in a similar group where I used to live.
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: Could you tell me something about your activities, please?
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: Of course.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: Well we have a mixture of regular activities and special events.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: One of the regular ones is trying to keep the beach free of litter.
audioscript.speaker: PETER
audioscript.explain: Q1: The passage says one regular activity is *'trying to keep the beach free of litter'* — **'free of'** means **'does not have'**. So the answer is **litter**.

audioscript.text: A few of us spend a couple of hours a month on it.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: And it's awful how much there is to clear.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: I wish people would be more responsible and take it home with them.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: I totally agree.
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: I'd be happy to help with that.
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: Is it OK to take dogs?
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: I'm afraid not, as they're banned from the beach itself.
audioscript.speaker: PETER
audioscript.explain: Q2: Jan asks if she can take dogs, and Peter says *'I'm afraid not, as they're banned from the beach itself'* — **'banned'** means **'no'**. So the answer is **dogs**.

audioscript.text: You can take them along the cliffs though, and children are welcome.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: We also manage a nature reserve, and there's a lot to do there all year round.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: Uh. For example, because it's a popular place to visit, we spend a lot of time looking after the paths.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: And making sure they're in good condition for walking.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: I could certainly help with that.
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: Good.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: And we have a program of creating new habitats there.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: We've just finished making and installing nesting boxes for birds to use, and next we're going to work on encouraging insects.
audioscript.speaker: PETER
audioscript.explain: Q3: Peter says *'next we're going to work on encouraging insects'* — **'encouraging'** here means **'attracting'** them to the reserve. So the answer is **insects**.

audioscript.text: They're important for the biodiversity of the reserve.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: They certainly are.
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: Oh, and we're also running a project to identify the different species of butterflies that visit the reserve.
audioscript.speaker: PETER
audioscript.explain: Q4: The group is *'running a project to identify the different species of butterflies'* — **'identifying types of'** matches **'identifying the different species of'**. So the answer is **butterflies**.

audioscript.text: You might be interested in taking part in that.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: Sure, I was involved in something similar where I used to live, counting all the species of moths.
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: I'd enjoy that.
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: Another job we're doing at the reserve is replacing the wall on the southern side.
audioscript.speaker: PETER
audioscript.explain: Q5: Peter mentions *'replacing the wall on the southern side'* — **'replacing'** means **'building a new'** one because the old one was damaged. So the answer is **wall**.

audioscript.text: Between the parking area and our woodshed, it was badly damaged in a storm last month.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: OK.
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Then, as I said, we have a program of events as well, both at the weekend and during the week.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: I presume you have guided walks.
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: I'd like to get to know the local countryside, as I'm new to the area.
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: Yes, we do.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: The next walk is to Ruston Island a week on Saturday.
audioscript.speaker: PETER
audioscript.explain: Q6: The walk is *'to Ruston Island'* — you walk across the sands and **'reach'** the island. So the answer is **island**.

audioscript.text: We'll be meeting in the car park at Dunsmore Beach at low tide.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: That's when the sands are dry enough for us to walk to the island without getting wet.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: Sounds good.
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: The island's a great place to explore. It's quite small, and it's got a range of habitats.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: It's also an ideal location for seeing seals just off the coast or even on the beach.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: OK. And is there anything we should bring?
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: Like a picnic for instance.
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: Yes, do bring one, as it's a full-day walk, and of course it'll be wet walking across and back, so make sure your boots are waterproof.
audioscript.speaker: PETER
audioscript.explain: Q7: Peter says *'make sure your boots are waterproof'* — **'waterproof'** is the **'appropriate'** quality for the wet walk. So the answer is **boots**.

audioscript.text: I must buy a new pair.
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: There's a hole in one of my current ones.
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: Well, I'd definitely like to come on the walk.
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: Great.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: Then later this month, we're having a one-day woodwork session in Hopton Wood.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: I've never tried that before.
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: Is it OK for beginners to take part?
audioscript.speaker: JAN
audioscript.explain: Q8: Jan asks *'Is it OK for beginners to take part?'* and Peter says definitely — **'take part'** means **'participate'**. So the answer is **beginners**.

audioscript.text: Definitely, there'll be a couple of experts leading the session, and we keep the number of participants down, so you'll get as much help as you need.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: Excellent! I'd love to be able to make chairs.
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: Ha. That's probably too ambitious for one day!
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: You'll be starting with wooden spoons, and of course learning how to use the tools, and anything you make is yours to take home with you.
audioscript.speaker: PETER
audioscript.explain: Q9: Peter says *'You'll be starting with wooden spoons'* — **'making'** spoons **'out of wood'** matches **'wooden spoons'**. So the answer is **spoons**.

audioscript.text: That sounds like fun.
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: When is it?
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: It's on the 17th, from 10 a.m. until 3.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: There's a charge of £35 including lunch,
audioscript.speaker: PETER
audioscript.explain: Q10: The passage says *'There's a charge of £35 including lunch'* — this is the cost **'no camping'** because camping costs £40. So the answer is **35**.

audioscript.text: or £40, if you want to camp in the wood.
audioscript.speaker: PETER

audioscript.text: I should think I'll come home the same day.
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: Well, I'd certainly like to join the group.
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: It sounds like you've...
audioscript.speaker: JAN

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers to part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Part 2, you will hear a tour guide, Lou Miller, speaking to a group of people about a boat trip they are going to take around the Australian island of Tasmania.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: So, hello everyone, my name is Lou Miller, and I'm going to be your tour guide today, as we take this fantastic boat trip around the Tasmanian coast.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: Before we set off, I just want to tell you a few things about our journey.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: Our boats aren't huge, as you can see, we already have three staff members on board.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: And on top of that, we can transport a further 15 people, that's you, around the coastline.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: But please note, if there are more than 9 people on either side of the boat, we'll move some of you over.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER
audioscript.explain: Q11: The guide says *'if there are more than 9 people on either side of the boat, we'll move some of you over'* — this means the **maximum** allowed on each side is **9**. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: Ha, otherwise all 18 of us will end up in the sea.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: We've recently upgraded all our boats.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: They used to be jet black, but our new ones now have these comfortable dark red seats and a light green exterior.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER
audioscript.explain: Q12: The passage says the new boats have *'a light green exterior'* — **'exterior'** means the outside colour. The old boats were jet black, but the question asks about the tour boats now. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: In order to stand out from others and help promote our company.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: This gives our boats a rather unique appearance, don't you think?
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: We offer you a free lunch box during the trip.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: And we have three types.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: Lunch Box 1 contains ham and tomato sandwiches.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: Lunch Box 2 contains a cheddar cheese roll.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER
audioscript.explain: Q13: Lunch Box 1 has ham, and Lunch Box 3 has tuna — both are meat or fish. Lunch Box 2 contains only *'a cheddar cheese roll'* — cheese is not meat or fish. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: And lunch box 3 is salad based, and also contains eggs and tuna.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: All three lunch boxes also have a packet of crisps and chocolate bar inside.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: Please let staff know which lunch box you prefer.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: I'm sure I don't have to ask you not to throw anything into the sea.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: We don't have any bins to put litter in, but Jess, myself or Ray, our other guide, will collect it from you after lunch.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER
audioscript.explain: Q14: The guide says *'We don't have any bins'* and that staff will *'collect it from you after lunch'* — **'collect it'** means you should **hand it to a member of staff**. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: And put it all in a large plastic sack.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: The engine on the boat makes quite a lot of noise, so before we head off, let me tell you a few things about what you're going to see.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: This area is famous for its ancient lighthouse, which you'll see from the boat as we turn past the first little island.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: It was built in 1838 to protect sailors, as a number of shipwrecks had led to significant loss of life.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER
audioscript.explain:
Q15: The guide explains the lighthouse was built *'to protect sailors'* after shipwrecks — this is **why it was built**. He also says workers were *'mainly prison convicts'* until families took over — this is **who staffed it**. So the answers are **A** and **D**.

audioscript.text: The construction itself was complicated, as some of the original drawings kept by the local council show.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: It sits right on top of the cliffs in a very isolated spot.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: In the 19th century, there were many jobs there, such as polishing the brass lamps, chopping firewood, and cleaning windows that kept lighthouse keepers busy.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: These workers were mainly prison convicts until the middle of that century, when ordinary families willing to live in such circumstances took over.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: Some of you have asked me what creatures we can expect to see.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: I know everyone loves the penguins, but they're very shy, and unfortunately tend to hide from passing boats.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: But you might see birds in the distance, such as sea eagles flying around the cliff edges where they nest.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER

audioscript.text: When we get to the rocky area inhabited by fur seals, we'll stop and watch them swimming around the coast.
audioscript.speaker: LOU MILLER
audioscript.explain:

audioscript.text: Part 4, you will hear an anthropology student giving a presentation on spiral path designs known as labyrinths.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Labyrinths have existed for well over 4,000 years.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Labyrinths and labyrinthine symbols have been found in regions as diverse as modern day Turkey.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Ireland, Greece and India.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: There are various designs of labyrinth, but what they all have in common is a winding spiral path, which leads to a central area.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: There is one starting point at the entrance, and the goal is to reach the central area.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Finding your way through a labyrinth involves many twists and turns.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But it's not possible to get lost, as there is only one single path.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In modern times, the word labyrinth has taken on a different meaning, and is often used as a synonym for a maze.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: A maze is quite different.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As it is a kind of puzzle with an intricate network of paths.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says a maze *'is a kind of puzzle'* — the question asks what type of thing a maze is. So the answer is **puzzle**.

audioscript.text: Mazes became fashionable in the 15th and 16th centuries in Europe, and can still be found in the gardens of great houses and palaces.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The paths are usually surrounded by thick high hedges, so that it's not possible to see over them.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Entering a maze usually involves getting lost a few times.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Before using logic to work out the pattern and find your way to the center, and then out again.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage says *'using logic to work out the pattern'* is how you find your way — **'logic'** is what you need to navigate. So the answer is **logic**.

audioscript.text: There are lots of dead ends and paths which lead you back to where you started.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The word maze is believed to come from a Scandinavian word for a state of confusion.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says the word maze comes from a Scandinavian word for *'a state of confusion'* — a **'state of confusion'** is a feeling. So the answer is **confusion**.

audioscript.text: This is where the word amazing comes from.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Labyrinths on the other hand have a very different function, although people now often refer to things they find complicated as labyrinths.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This is not how they were seen in the past.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The winding spiral of the labyrinth has been used for centuries as a metaphor for life's journey.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It served as a spiritual reminder that there is purpose and meaning to our lives.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And helped to give people a sense of direction.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Labyrinths are thought to encourage a feeling of calm, and have been used as a meditation and prayer tool in many cultures over many centuries.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says labyrinths have been used as a *'meditation and prayer tool'* — the question already gives you **'prayer'**, so the missing word is **meditation**.

audioscript.text: The earliest examples of the labyrinth spiral pattern have been found carved into stone from Sardinia to Scandinavia, from Arizona to India.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says the earliest examples were *'carved into stone'* — the question asks about ancient carvings on what material. So the answer is **stone**.

audioscript.text: To Africa.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In Europe, these spiral carvings date from the late Bronze Age.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The Native American Pima tribe wove baskets with a circular labyrinth design.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That depicted their own cosmology, in ancient Greece, the labyrinth spiral was used on coins around 4,000 years ago.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage says in ancient Greece, the labyrinth spiral *'was used on coins'* — the question asks what the Greeks used the symbol on. So the answer is **coins**.

audioscript.text: Labyrinths made of mosaics were commonly found in bathhouses, villas, and tombs throughout the Roman Empire.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In Northern Europe, there were actual physical labyrinths designed for walking on.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: These were cut into the turf or grass, usually in a circular pattern.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The origin of these walking labyrinths remains unclear, but they were probably used for fertility rites, which may date back thousands of years.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: 11 examples of turf labyrinths survive today.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Including the largest one at Saffron Walden in England, which used to have a large tree in the middle of it.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says the largest turf labyrinth *'used to have a large tree in the middle of it'* — the question asks what big thing was at its centre. So the answer is **tree**.

audioscript.text: More recently, labyrinths have experienced something of a revival.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Some believe that walking a labyrinth promotes healing and mindfulness, and there are those who believe in its emotional and physical benefits,
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: which include slower breathing and a restored sense of balance and perspective.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage says benefits include *'slower breathing'* — the question asks what rate can be reduced, and **'breathing'** rate matches. So the answer is **breathing**.

audioscript.text: This idea has become so popular that labyrinths have been laid into the floors of spas, wellness centers, and even prisons in recent years.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: A pamphlet at Colorado Children's Hospital informs patients that 'walking a labyrinth can often calm people in the midst of a crisis'.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And apparently, it's not only patients who benefit.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Many visitors find walking a labyrinth less stressful than sitting in a corridor or waiting room.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Some doctors even walk the labyrinth during their breaks.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In some hospitals, patients who can't walk can have a paper finger labyrinth brought to their bed.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage says patients who can't walk can have a *'paper finger labyrinth'* — the question asks what material these are made from. So the answer is **paper**.

audioscript.text: The science behind the theory is a little sketchy, but there are dozens of small-scale studies which support claims about the benefits of labyrinths.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: For example, one study found that walking a labyrinth provided 'short-term calming, relaxation and relief from anxiety' for Alzheimer's patients.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says walking a labyrinth provided *'relief from anxiety'* for Alzheimer's patients — **'relief from'** means they experience less of it. So the answer is **anxiety**.

audioscript.text: So what is it about labyrinths that makes their appeal so universal?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Hello, Jane Fairbanks speaking.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: Oh, good morning.

audioscript.text: My name is Frank Pritchard.
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: And I gather you coordinate voluntary work in the village.
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: That's right.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: What sort of thing could I do?
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: Well, we need help with the village library.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: We borrow books from the town library, and individuals also donate them.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: So one thing you could do is get involved in collecting them.
audioscript.speaker: JANE
audioscript.explain: Q1: The passage says you could *'get involved in collecting them'* — **'them'** refers to the books. So the help needed is **collecting** books.

audioscript.text: If you've got a car, that is.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: Yes, that's no problem.
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: The times are pretty flexible, so we can arrange it to suit you.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: Oh, another thing is the records that we keep of the books we're given.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: And those we borrow and need to return to the town library, it would be very useful to have another person to help keep them up to date.
audioscript.speaker: JANE
audioscript.explain: Q2: The passage says it would be useful to have help *'keep them up to date'* — **'them'** means the **records** of books. So the answer is **records**.

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: I'm used to working on a computer, I presume they're computerized?
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: Oh, yes.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: Is the library purpose built?
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: I haven't noticed it when I've walked around the village.
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: No, we simply have the use of a room in the village hall, the West Room.
audioscript.speaker: JANE
audioscript.explain: Q3: The passage directly names the room: *'the West Room'*. So the library is in the **West** Room.

audioscript.text: It's on the left as you go in.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: I must go and have a look inside the hall.
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: Yes, it's a nice building.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: Do you run a lunch club in the village for elderly people?
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: I know a lot of places do.
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: Yes, we have a very successful club.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: I could help with transport, if that's of any use.
audioscript.speaker: FRANK
audioscript.explain: Q4: The man offers: *'I could help with transport'*. So for the lunch club, he can help by providing **transport**.

audioscript.text: Oh, definitely.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: People come to the club from neighboring villages, and we're always in need of more drivers.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: And does the club have groups that focus on a particular hobby too?
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: I could get involved in one or two, particularly if there are any art groups.
audioscript.speaker: FRANK
audioscript.explain: Q5: The man asks about hobby groups, *'particularly if there are any art groups'*. So the hobby he mentions is **art**.

audioscript.text: Excellent.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: I'll find out where we need help and get back to you.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: Fine.
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: What about help for individual residents?
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: Do you arrange that at all?
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: Yes, we do it as a one-off.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: Oh, in fact, there's Mrs Carroll.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: She needs a lift to the hospital next week, and we're struggling to find someone.
audioscript.speaker: JANE
audioscript.explain: Q6: The passage says Mrs Carroll *'needs a lift to the hospital'*. So she needs to be taken to the **hospital**.

audioscript.text: When's her appointment?
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: On Tuesday, it would take the whole morning.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: I could do that.
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: Oh, that would be great.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: Thank you.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: And also next week, we're arranging to have some work done to Mr Selsbury's house before he moves, as he isn't healthy enough to do it himself.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: We've got some people to decorate his kitchen.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: But if you could do some weeding in his garden, that would be wonderful.
audioscript.speaker: JANE
audioscript.explain: Q7: The passage asks if he could *'do some weeding in his garden'*. So the work is in the **garden**.

audioscript.text: OK, I'd enjoy that, and presumably the day and time are flexible.
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: Oh, yes.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: Just say when would suit you best, and we'll let Mr Selsbury know.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: Good.
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 8 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 8 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: The volunteers group also organizes monthly social events, which is a great way to meet other people, of course.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: Uh huh.
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: So, next month on the 19th of October, we're holding a quiz.
audioscript.speaker: JANE
audioscript.explain: Q8: The passage says on the 19th of October, *'we're holding a quiz'*. So the event is a **quiz**.

audioscript.text: A couple of residents are great at planning unusual ones, and we always fill the village hall.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: That sounds like fun.
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: Can I do anything to help?
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: Well, because of the number of people, we need plenty of refreshments for halfway through.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: So, if you could provide any, we'd be grateful.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: I'm sure I could.
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: I'll think about what to make and let you know.
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: Thank you.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: Then on November the 18th.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: We're holding a dance, also in the village hall.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: We've booked a band that specializes in music of the 1930s - they've been before.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: And we've had a lot of requests to bring them back.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: I'm not really a dancer, but I'd like to do something to help.
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: Well, we sell tickets in advance.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: And having an extra person to check them at the door as people arrive would be good.
audioscript.speaker: JANE
audioscript.explain: Q9: The passage says they need an extra person to *'check them at the door'* — **'them'** refers to the **tickets** sold in advance. So the help is checking **tickets**.

audioscript.text: It can be quite a bottleneck if everyone arrives at once.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: OK, I'm happy with that.
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: Oh. We're also arranging a New Year's Eve party.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: We're expecting that to be a really big event, so instead of the village hall, it'll be held in the Mountfort hotel.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: The mountfort, MOUNTFORT Hotel.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: It isn't in Southoe itself, but it's only a couple of miles away.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: The hotel will be providing dinner, and we've booked a band.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: The one thing we haven't got yet is a poster.
audioscript.speaker: JANE
audioscript.explain: Q10: The passage says the one thing they haven't got yet is *'a poster'*, and asks if he can design it. So the help needed is designing the **poster**.

audioscript.text: That isn't something you could do by any chance, is it?
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: Well, actually, yes.
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: Uh. Before I retired, I was a graphic designer, so that's right up my street.
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: Perfect, I'll give you the details, and then perhaps you could send me a draft.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: Of course.
audioscript.speaker: FRANK

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers to part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Part 2, you will hear a guide at a tourist attraction called Oniton Hall talking to a group of visitors.

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.

audioscript.text: Good morning, and welcome to Oniton Hall, one of the largest estates in the area.
audioscript.speaker: NICK

audioscript.text: My name's Nick, and I'm one of the guides.
audioscript.speaker: NICK

audioscript.text: I'll give you a brief introduction to the estate while you're sitting down, and then we'll walk round.
audioscript.speaker: NICK

audioscript.text: The estate consists of the house, gardens, park land and farm, and it dates back to the 14th century.
audioscript.speaker: NICK

audioscript.text: The original house was replaced in the late 17th century.
audioscript.speaker: NICK

audioscript.text: And of course, it has had a large number of owners.
audioscript.speaker: NICK

audioscript.text: Almost all of them have left their mark, generally by adding new rooms.
audioscript.speaker: NICK
audioscript.explain: Q11: The passage says *'Almost all of them have left their mark, generally by adding new rooms'* — **'adding new rooms'** means making changes to the **house**. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: Like the ballroom and conservatory, or by demolishing others.
audioscript.speaker: NICK

audioscript.text: The farm looks much as it's always done, although the current owner has done a great deal of work to the flower beds.
audioscript.speaker: NICK

audioscript.text: In the 17th century, the estate was owned by a very wealthy man called Sir Edward Downes.
audioscript.speaker: NICK

audioscript.text: His intention was to escape from the world of politics.
audioscript.speaker: NICK

audioscript.text: After years as an active politician, and to build a new house worthy of his big collection of books, paintings and sculptures.
audioscript.speaker: NICK

audioscript.text: He broke off contact with his former political allies and hosted meetings of creative and literary people, like painters and poets.
audioscript.speaker: NICK
audioscript.explain: Q12: The passage says Sir Edward *'hosted meetings of creative and literary people, like painters and poets'* — **'creative and literary people'** means **artists and writers**. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: Unusually for his time, he didn't care whether his guests were rich or poor, as long as they had talent.
audioscript.speaker: NICK

audioscript.text: Big houses like Oniton had dozens of servants until the 1920s or 30s, and we've tried to show what their working lives were like.
audioscript.speaker: NICK

audioscript.text: Photographs of course don't give much of an idea, so instead, as you go round the house, you'll see volunteers dressed up as nineteenth-century servants, going about their work.
audioscript.speaker: NICK
audioscript.explain: Q13: The passage says you'll see *'volunteers dressed up as nineteenth-century servants'* — **'dressed up'** means they are **people in costume**. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: They'll explain what they're doing, and tell you their recipes, or what tools they're using.
audioscript.speaker: NICK

audioscript.text: We've just introduced this feature to replace the audio guide.
audioscript.speaker: NICK

audioscript.text: We used to have available.
audioscript.speaker: NICK

audioscript.text: I see there are a number of children here with you today.
audioscript.speaker: NICK

audioscript.text: So, what about the Emporium Theater's production of the play?
audioscript.speaker: ED

audioscript.text: I thought some things worked really well, but there were some problems too.
audioscript.speaker: GEMMA

audioscript.text: Yeah.
audioscript.speaker: ED

audioscript.text: What about the set for example?
audioscript.speaker: ED

audioscript.text: I think it was visually really stunning.
audioscript.speaker: GEMMA

audioscript.text: I'd say that was probably the most memorable thing about this production.
audioscript.speaker: GEMMA

audioscript.speaker: ED

audioscript.text: The set design was really amazing, but actually I have seen similar ideas used in other productions.
audioscript.speaker: ED

audioscript.text: Hmm. What about the lighting?

audioscript.text: Some of the scenes were so dimly lit, it was quite hard to see.
audioscript.speaker: GEMMA

audioscript.text: I didn't dislike it.

audioscript.text: It helped to change the mood of the quieter scenes.
audioscript.speaker: ED

audioscript.text: Yeah.

audioscript.speaker: GEMMA

audioscript.text: But I thought they were wasted, because the music didn't have much impact in Acts 2 and 3.
audioscript.speaker: GEMMA
audioscript.explain: Q26: One student says the musicians were brilliant but *'the music didn't have much impact in Acts 2 and 3'* — this means they were **disappointed**. The other student agrees it was a shame. So the answer is **E**.

audioscript.text: They were speaking too fast.

audioscript.text: It was a problem I agree, but I thought it was because they weren't speaking loudly enough, especially at key points in the play.

audioscript.explain: Q27: One student says the problem with the actors was *'speaking too fast'*. The other agrees it was a problem but thinks it was because they *'weren't speaking loudly enough'*. They agree there is an issue, but **disagree about why** it happened. So the answer is **F**.

audioscript.text: I actually didn't have a problem with that.
audioscript.speaker: GEMMA

audioscript.speaker: ED

audioscript.text: Definitely.
audioscript.speaker: GEMMA

audioscript.text: It's made me realize how relevant the play still is.
audioscript.speaker: GEMMA

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: ED

audioscript.text: I mean a lot's changed since Shakespeare's time, but in many ways nothing's changed.
audioscript.speaker: ED

audioscript.text: There are always disagreements and tension between teenagers and their parents.
audioscript.speaker: ED
audioscript.explain: Q28: The students say the play is still relevant because of *'disagreements and tension between teenagers and their parents'* — this is about **problems that families experience**. They say all young people can relate to this. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: Yes.
audioscript.speaker: GEMMA

audioscript.text: That's something all young people can relate to, more than the violence and the extreme emotions in the play.

audioscript.text: Really interesting.
audioscript.speaker: GEMMA

audioscript.text: I expected to find it more challenging, but I could follow the story pretty well.

audioscript.text: The characters have such depth.

audioscript.text: Right.

audioscript.text: Part 4, you will hear a lecturer on a languages course talking about the impact of digital technology on Icelandic, the native language of Iceland.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Right, everyone.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Let's make a start.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Over the past few sessions, we've been considering the reasons why some world languages are in decline.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And today, I'm going to introduce another factor that affects languages, and the speakers of those languages, and that's technology, and in particular digital technology.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In order to illustrate its effect, I'm going to focus on the Icelandic language, which is spoken by around 321,000 people.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says Icelandic *'is spoken by around 321,000 people'* — **'around'** means approximately. So the answer is **321,000**.

audioscript.text: Most of whom live in Iceland, an island in the North Atlantic Ocean.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The problem for this language is not the number of speakers, even though this number is small, nor is it about losing words to other languages such as English.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In fact, the vocabulary of Icelandic is continually increasing, because when speakers need a new word for something, they tend to create one, rather than borrowing from another language.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage says *'the vocabulary of Icelandic is continually increasing'* — **'continually increasing'** means it is still growing. So the answer is **vocabulary**.

audioscript.text: All this makes Icelandic quite a special language.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It's changed very little in the past millennium, yet it can handle 21st century concepts related to the use of computers and digital technology.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Take for example the word for web browser.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This is vafri in Icelandic, which comes from the verb 'to wander'.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: I can't think of a more appropriate term, because that's exactly what you do mentally when you browse the internet.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Then there's an Icelandic word for podcast, which is too hard to pronounce, and so on.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage gives examples of computer-based words, mentioning *'an Icelandic word for podcast'* after web browser. So the answer is **podcast**.

audioscript.text: Icelandic then is alive and growing, but, and it's a big but, young Icelanders spend a great deal of time in the digital world, and this world is predominantly English.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Think about smartphones.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage asks you to *'Think about smartphones'* as an example of digital technology young people use. So the answer is **smartphones**.

audioscript.text: They didn't even exist until comparatively recently, but today young people use them all the time to read books, watch TV or films.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Play games, listen to music, and so on.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Obviously, this is a good thing in many respects, because it promotes their bilingual skills.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says using digital technology *'promotes their bilingual skills'* — **'promotes'** here means they are becoming more bilingual. So the answer is **bilingual**.

audioscript.text: But the extent of the influence of English in the virtual world is staggering.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And it's all happening really fast.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: For their parents and grandparents, the change is less concerning, because they already have their native-speaker skills in Icelandic.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But for young speakers, well, the outcome is a little troubling.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: For example, teachers have found that playground conversations in Icelandic secondary schools can be conducted entirely in English, while teachers of much younger children have reported situations where their classes find it easier to say what is in a picture using English, rather than Icelandic.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain:
Q36: The passage says *'playground conversations in Icelandic secondary schools can be conducted entirely in English'* — this is where they have discussions using only English. So the answer is **playground**.

Q37: The passage says younger children *'find it easier to say what is in a picture using English'* — **'say what is in'** means identify the content. So the answer is **picture**.

audioscript.text: The very real and worrying consequence of all this, is that the young generation in Iceland is at risk of losing its mother tongue.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Of course, this is happening to other European languages too, but while internet companies might be willing to offer say French options in their systems.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It's much harder for them to justify the expense of doing the same for a language that has a population the size of a French town, such as Nice.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The other drawback of Icelandic is the grammar, which is significantly more complex than in most languages.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage says *'the other drawback of Icelandic is the grammar, which is significantly more complex'* — **'complex'** means complicated. So the answer is **grammar**.

audioscript.text: At the moment, the tech giants are simply not interested in tackling this.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So, what is the Icelandic government doing about this?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Well, large sums of money are being allocated to a language technology fund that it is hoped will lead to the development of Icelandic sourced apps.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And other social media and digital systems, but clearly this is going to be an uphill struggle.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: On the positive side, they know that Icelandic is still the official language of education and government.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It has survived for well over 1,000 years, and the experts predict that its future in this nation state is sound, and will continue to be so.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: However, there's no doubt that it's becoming an inevitable second choice in young people's lives.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This raises important questions when you consider how much of the past is tied up in a language.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Will young Icelanders lose their sense of their own identity?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage asks *'Will young Icelanders lose their sense of their own identity?'* — this is the government's worry about what they may lose. So the answer is **identity**.

audioscript.text: Another issue that concerns the government of Iceland is this. If children are learning two languages through different routes.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Neither of which they are fully fluent in.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says children learn two languages, *'Neither of which they are fully fluent in'* — **'fully fluent'** means being completely able to speak a language. So the answer is **fluent**.

audioscript.text: Will they be able to express themselves properly?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Good afternoon.
audioscript.speaker: MRS CARTER

audioscript.text: My name's Mrs Carter, and I run the before and after school extended hours childcare service.
audioscript.speaker: MRS CARTER

audioscript.text: I hope you've had a chance to have a good look around the school, and talk to staff and pupils.
audioscript.speaker: MRS CARTER

audioscript.text: I know that many of you are interested in using our childcare service when your child joins the school, and perhaps you already know something about it, but for those that don't, I'll go through the main details now.
audioscript.speaker: MRS CARTER

audioscript.text: We offer child care for children from the ages of 4 to 11, both before and after school.
audioscript.speaker: MRS CARTER

audioscript.text: I know that many parents who work find this service invaluable.
audioscript.speaker: MRS CARTER

audioscript.text: You can leave your child with us, safe in the knowledge that they will be extremely well cared for.
audioscript.speaker: MRS CARTER

audioscript.text: We are insured to provide care for up to 70 children, although we rarely have this many attending at any one session.
audioscript.speaker: MRS CARTER

audioscript.text: Part 3, you will hear Holly, a student on an events management course, talking to her tutor about her work placement.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Hello, Doctor Green.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: I'm here to talk to you about my work placement.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: Oh, yes, it's Holly, isn't it?
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: Yes.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: So, which work placement have you chosen?
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: I decided to go for the Orion Stadium placement.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: The event I'll be managing is one where I'm helping to set up a sports competition for primary school children.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: Yep, that's always a popular placement, even though it can be tougher than you think working with children.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: I know, but it's the fresh air that attracts me.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY
audioscript.explain: Q21: Holly says *'it's the fresh air that attracts me'* — **'fresh air'** means being **outdoors**. She also says *'organizing something indoors doesn't have the same appeal'*, which confirms she prefers outside. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: Organizing something indoors doesn't have the same appeal, even though it might be fun.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: OK, so obviously safety is going to be one of your key concerns for this event.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: Yes, I've already thought about that.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: I'll need to make sure none of the equipment's damaged.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: Uh. Well you'll be working with schools, so the equipment will be their responsibility.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: However, the grounds and what goes on there will be yours.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: Oh, I see.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: That'll include keeping everyone within the boundary once they're in their kit and on the field.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: Exactly.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: You'll need to inspect areas like changing rooms as well, for anything someone can trip over.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: But your main priority will be not to lose anyone.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR
audioscript.explain: Q22: Dr Green says *'your main priority will be not to lose anyone'* — **'not to lose anyone'** means keeping children inside the stadium. He mentions other safety points like checking changing rooms, but he calls this the **main priority**. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: Uh. Right.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: I'll need staff to help with that.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: And don't forget about the spectators.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: Hmm. I was thinking that many of them will be parents who could help run the event.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: I wouldn't rely on that.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: They'll be more interested in filming their children than volunteering.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: I'll need to make sure they don't interfere with events doing that.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: And that's not always easy, especially when a proud parent's trying to get a snap of their child,
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR
audioscript.explain: Q23: Dr Green says *'that's not always easy, especially when a proud parent's trying to get a snap of their child'* — **'not always easy'** means they can be **hard to manage**. He warns that parents will be more interested in filming than volunteering, so they are not useful helpers. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: and you want them to move elsewhere.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: OK, uh, what about the scheduling?
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: With sporting events, there are all sorts of things that can alter the timetable.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: Like rain for instance, though so far we've always been lucky with that.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: Yeah, and I was thinking about what to do if someone got hurt as well.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: I know that last year that caused a terrible delay.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY
audioscript.explain: Q24: Holly says *'I know that last year that caused a terrible delay'* — she is talking about what to do if someone got hurt. So **an injury** affected the schedule in the past. Rain is mentioned as a possible problem, but Dr Green says they have been lucky with it. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: You have to be prepared for such things.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: Oh, what if a match ends in a draw?
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: Do you let the teams keep going until someone wins?
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: That'll be up to you, and again, you need to plan for it.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now, the aim of your work placement is to give you the opportunity to develop the skills that an events manager needs.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: So, let's talk about those a bit.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: Well, I think my communication skills are pretty good.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: I can talk on the phone to people, and book venues, and that kind of thing.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: Good.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: Just remember, it isn't only about what you say.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: If you meet someone face to face and want to persuade them to be a sponsor, for example.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR
audioscript.explain: Q25: Dr Green says if you meet someone face to face, you need to persuade them — Holly replies *'I'll dress up for that'*. **'Dress up'** means having a **smart appearance**. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: Oh, I'll dress up for that, sure.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY
audioscript.explain: Q25: Dr Green says if you meet someone face to face, you need to persuade them — Holly replies *'I'll dress up for that'*. **'Dress up'** means having a **smart appearance**. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: Good. Let's go on to think about your organizational skills.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: You're working in a very people-based industry, and that means things won't always go to plan.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: I guess it's being prepared to make changes that matters.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY
audioscript.explain: Q26: Holly says *'it's being prepared to make changes that matters'* — **'being prepared to make changes'** means **being flexible**. Dr Green agrees with her. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: That's right.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: You may have to make an on-the-spot change to a timetable because of a problem you hadn't anticipated.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: Just do it! OK.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: How's your time management these days?
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: I'm working on it.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: I'm certainly better when I have a deadline, which is why this work suits me.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: Yes, but it's how you respond as that deadline approaches.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: I know I've got to look calm, even if I'm in a panic.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY
audioscript.explain: Q27: Holly says *'I know I've got to look calm, even if I'm in a panic'* — **'look calm'** when you are panicking means **hiding your emotions**. Dr Green tells her no one must know she is under pressure. So the answer is **D**.

audioscript.text: Just think to yourself, no one must know I'm under pressure.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: Yeah, even though I'm multitasking like crazy.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: Another skill that events managers need is creativity.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: Often your client has what we call the big picture idea, but it's up to the events manager to think of all the fine points that go to making it work.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR
audioscript.explain: Q28: Dr Green says the events manager must think of *'all the fine points that go to making it work'* — **'fine points'** means **details**. Holly agrees she needs to *'fill in all the gaps'*, which is the same idea. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: Right, so I need to listen carefully to that idea, and then fill in all the gaps.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: That's right, and you'll have a team working under you.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: So another key skill is leadership.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: Your team may have lots of ideas too, but you've got to make the ultimate choices.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: Do we have refreshments inside or out for example?
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: Isn't it better to be democratic?
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: It's a nice idea, but you have the ultimate responsibility.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: So believe in what you think best.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR
audioscript.explain: Q29: Dr Green says *'believe in what you think best'* — this means **trusting your own views**. He tells Holly she must make the ultimate choices, even if the team has ideas. So the answer is **F**.

audioscript.text: Be prepared to say yes, that's a good idea, but it won't work here.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: I see what you mean.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: What about the networking side of things?
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: I know it's an area that a lot of students worry about, because we don't have much experience to offer others.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: But even without it, you can still be an interesting person with useful ideas.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: And the more people you impress, the better.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: I guess that will help me when I apply for a real job.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: Exactly.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: Think ahead, remember what your ambitions are.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR
audioscript.explain: Q30: Dr Green says *'think ahead, remember what your ambitions are'* — **'think ahead'** and **'ambitions'** mean **thinking of the future**. He tells Holly to keep her ambitions in mind. So the answer is **H**.

audioscript.text: And keep them in mind.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: Uh. Definitely.
audioscript.speaker: HOLLY

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 3.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

body.title: Bird Migration Theory

audioscript.text: Part 4, you will hear a zoology student giving a presentation on bird migration.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Scientists believe that a majority of the Earth's bird population migrate in some fashion or other.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Some travel seasonally for relatively short distances.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Such as birds that move from their winter habitats in lowlands to mountaintops for the summers. Others, like the Arctic Tern, travel more than 25,000 miles seasonally.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Between the northern and southern poles.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Bird migration has been studied over many centuries through a variety of observations, but until relatively recently, where birds went to in the winter was considered something of a mystery.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The lack of modern science and technology led to many theories that we now recognize as error filled, and even somewhat amusing.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Take hibernation theory for example, 2000 years ago, it was commonly believed that when birds left an area, they went underwater to hibernate in the seas and oceans.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Another theory for the regular appearance and disappearance of birds was that they spent winter hidden in mud, till the weather changed and food became abundant again.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says birds *'spent winter hidden in mud'* — the question asks where they buried themselves. So the answer is **mud**.

audioscript.text: The theory that some birds hibernate persisted until experiments were done on caged birds in the 1940s which demonstrated that birds have no hibernation instinct.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: One of the earliest naturalists and philosophers from ancient Greece was Aristotle, who was the first writer to discuss the disappearance and reappearance of some bird species.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: At certain times of year, he developed the theory of transmutation, the seasonal change of one species into another, by observing redstarts and robins.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: He observed that in the autumn, small birds called redstarts began to lose their feathers, which convinced Aristotle that they changed into robins for the winter.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage says redstarts *'began to lose their feathers'* — **'lose'** here means the same as the question's **'loss of'**. So the answer is **feathers**.

audioscript.text: And back into redstarts in the summer.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: These assumptions are understandable, given that this pair of species are similar in shape.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says the two species *'are similar in shape'* — **'similar'** means they have a like **'shape'**. So the answer is **shape**.

audioscript.text: But are a classic example of an incorrect interpretation based on correct observations.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The most bizarre theory was put forward by an English amateur scientist, Charles Morton, in the 17th century.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: He wrote a surprisingly well regarded paper.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Claiming that birds migrate to the moon and back every year.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says Charles Morton claimed birds *'migrate to the moon and back'* — the question asks where they fly to. So the answer is **moon**.

audioscript.text: He came to this conclusion as the only logical explanation for the total disappearance of some species.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: One of the key moments in the development of migration theory came in 1822 when a white stork was shot in Germany.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This particular stork made history because of the long spear in its neck, which incredibly had not killed it.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says the stork had *'the long spear in its neck'* — the question asks where the spear was. So the answer is **neck**.

audioscript.text: Everyone immediately realized this spear was definitely not European.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It turned out to be a spear from a tribe in central Africa.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This was a truly defining moment in the history of ornithology.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Because it was the first evidence that storks spend their winters in sub-Saharan Africa.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage says this was *'the first evidence that storks spend their winters in sub-Saharan Africa'* — the question says previously there was no proof. So the answer is **evidence**.

audioscript.text: You can still see the arrow stork in the zoological collection of the university of Rostock in Germany.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: People gradually became aware that European birds moved south in autumn and north in summer, but didn't know much about it until the practice of catching birds.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And putting rings on their legs became established.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Before this, very little information was available about the actual destinations of particular species.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says before ringing, little was known about *'the actual destinations of particular species'* — **'destinations'** means where they go, matching the question's **'journeys'**. So the answer is **destinations**.

audioscript.text: And how they traveled there.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: People speculated that larger birds provided a kind of taxi service for smaller birds by carrying them on their backs.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This idea came about, because it seemed impossible that small birds weighing only a few grams could fly over vast oceans.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage says small birds *'could fly over vast oceans'* — **'vast'** means huge, so the question's **'huge'** matches. So the answer is **oceans**.

audioscript.text: This idea was supported by observations of bird behavior, such as the harassment of larger birds by smaller birds.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The development of bird ringing, by a Danish school teacher, Hans Christian Cornelius Mortensen, made many discoveries possible.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This is still common practice today, and relies upon what is known as recovery.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage says ringing *'relies upon what is known as recovery'* — the question asks what the process is called. So the answer is **recovery**.

audioscript.text: This is when ringed birds are found dead in the place they have migrated to.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And identified.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Huge amounts of data were gathered in the early part of the 20th century, and for the first time in history, people understood where birds actually went to in winter.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In 1931, an atlas was published showing where the most common species of European birds migrated to.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says in 1931 *'an atlas was published'* showing migration — the question asks what was printed. So the answer is **atlas**.

audioscript.text: More recent theories about bird migration...
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Part 2, you will hear a training manager giving a talk to a group of senior staff from a hotel chain about the problem of high staff turnover.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: As many of you here today have worked in the hotel industry for some time, I'm sure you have experienced the problem of high staff turnover in your hotels.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Every hotel relies on having loyal and experienced members of staff who make sure that everything runs smoothly.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: If staff are constantly changing it can make life difficult for everyone.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But why do staff leave frequently in many hotels?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Of course, many hotel jobs such as cleaning are low skilled and are not well paid.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: A lot of managers think it's this, and the long hours that are the main causes of high staff turnover, but what they don't realize is that it's the lack of training in many hotel jobs.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q11: Many managers think staff leave because of **long hours** or **low pay**, but the passage says *'what they don't realize is that it's the lack of training'*. So the real reason managers are **unaware** of is **a lack of training**. The answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: Which is a huge factor.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So, what kind of problems does a high turnover of staff cause?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Well, having to recruit new staff all the time can be very time consuming.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And managers may have to cover some duties while waiting for new staff to arrive.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This means they don't have time to think about less immediate problems, such as how to improve their service.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q12: The passage says managers must cover duties, so they *'don't have time to think about less immediate problems'*. This means they are too busy with daily work — their **workload** has increased. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: When staff leave, it can also severely affect the colleagues they leave behind.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It has a negative effect on remaining staff, who may start to feel that they too should be thinking about leaving.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So what can be done to change this situation?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Firstly, managers should stop making basic errors, which leave their staff feeling upset and resentful.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: When organizing shifts, for example.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Make sure you never give certain staff preferential treatment.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q13: The passage warns managers to *'never give certain staff preferential treatment'*. **'Preferential treatment'** means treating some people better than others — the opposite of treating staff **equally**. So the mistake to avoid is **failing to treat staff equally**, answer **A**.

audioscript.text: All staff should be given some choice about when they work, and everyone should have to work some evening and weekend shifts.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: If you treat staff fairly, they'll be more likely to step in and help when extra staff are needed.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Keeping staff happy has other tangible benefits for the business.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Take the Dunwich Hotel as an example.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It had been experiencing a problem with staff complaints, and in order to deal with this, invested in staff training and improved staff conditions.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Not only did the level of complaints fall, but they also noticed a significant increase in the amount each customer spent during their stay.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q14: The passage says after changes, Dunwich Hotel saw *'a significant increase in the amount each customer spent'*. **'Amount each customer spent'** is the same as **spending per customer**. ***Don't confuse this with the fall in complaints*** — that was expected, but the **unexpected** benefit was the rise in spending. The answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: They have now introduced a customer loyalty scheme, which is going really well.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now, I'd like to look at some ways you can reduce staff turnover in your hotels, and I'll do this by giving some examples of hotels where I've done some training recently.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The Sun Club received feedback which showed that staff thought managers didn't value their opinions.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They weren't made to feel they were partners who were contributing to the success of the business as a whole.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This situation has changed.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Junior staff at all levels are regularly invited to meetings where their ideas are welcomed.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q15: The Sun Club now invites junior staff to meetings where *'their ideas are welcomed'*. This makes staff feel like valued partners, which improves **relationships and teamwork**. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: A year ago, The Portland recognized the need to invest in staff retention.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Their first step was to introduce a scheme for recognizing talent amongst their employees.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q16: The Portland introduced a scheme for *'recognizing talent'* and training those with *'management potential'*. This gives staff a path to grow in the company — that is **providing career opportunities**. The answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: The hope is that organizing training for individuals with management potential will encourage them to stay with the business.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: At Bluewater, managers decided to recognize 50 high achievers from across the company's huge hotel chain as a reward.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They're sent on an all-expenses-paid trip abroad every year.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q17: Bluewater Hotels sends high achievers on an *'all-expenses-paid trip abroad every year'*. A free trip is a reward, which is an **incentive and financial benefit**. The answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: Fun is an important element in the trips, but there's also the opportunity to learn something useful.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This year's trip included a visit to a brewery, where staff learned about the new beer that would be served in the hotel.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Pentlow Hotels identified that retention of junior reception staff was an issue in order to encourage them to see that working in a hotel could be worthwhile and rewarding, with good prospects, they introduced a management program.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q18: Pentlow Hotels introduced a *'management program'* and gave staff *'additional responsibilities'* and *'various roles'*. This shows them a future in the hotel — it is **providing career opportunities**. The answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: These staff were given additional responsibilities.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And the chance to work in various roles in the hotel.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Green Planet wanted to be seen as a caring employer. To make life easier for staff, many of whom had childcare responsibilities,
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: the hotel began issuing vouchers to help cover the cost of childcare.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q19: Green Planet began *'issuing vouchers to help cover the cost of childcare'*. Vouchers are like money to pay for something — this is an **incentive and financial benefit**. The answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: Louise Marsh at the Amesbury has one of the best staff retention rates in the business.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Since she joined the company, she's made a huge effort to achieve this.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: By creating a co-operative and supportive environment.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q20: Louise Marsh at the Amesbury created a *'co-operative and supportive environment'* where staff feel like *'family'*. This is all about **improving relationships and teamwork**. The answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: For her, the staff are part of a large family where everyone is valued.

audioscript.text: OK, now I'd like to...
