utterances.text: So, what kind of problems does a high turnover of staff cause?
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Well, having to recruit new staff all the time can be very time consuming.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: And managers may have to cover some duties while waiting for new staff to arrive.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: This means they don't have time to think about less immediate problems, such as how to improve their service.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q12: The passage says managers must cover duties, so they *'don't have time to think about less immediate problems'*. This means they are too busy with daily work — their **workload** has increased. So the answer is **A**.

utterances.text: When staff leave, it can also severely affect the colleagues they leave behind.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: It has a negative effect on remaining staff, who may start to feel that they too should be thinking about leaving.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: So what can be done to change this situation?
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Firstly, managers should stop making basic errors, which leave their staff feeling upset and resentful.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: When organizing shifts, for example.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Make sure you never give certain staff preferential treatment.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q13: The passage warns managers to *'never give certain staff preferential treatment'*. **'Preferential treatment'** means treating some people better than others — the opposite of treating staff **equally**. So the mistake to avoid is **failing to treat staff equally**, answer **A**.

utterances.text: All staff should be given some choice about when they work, and everyone should have to work some evening and weekend shifts.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: If you treat staff fairly, they'll be more likely to step in and help when extra staff are needed.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Keeping staff happy has other tangible benefits for the business.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Take the Dunwich Hotel as an example.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: It had been experiencing a problem with staff complaints, and in order to deal with this, invested in staff training and improved staff conditions.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Not only did the level of complaints fall, but they also noticed a significant increase in the amount each customer spent during their stay.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q14: The passage says after changes, Dunwich Hotel saw *'a significant increase in the amount each customer spent'*. **'Amount each customer spent'** is the same as **spending per customer**. ***Don't confuse this with the fall in complaints*** — that was expected, but the **unexpected** benefit was the rise in spending. The answer is **C**.

utterances.text: They have now introduced a customer loyalty scheme, which is going really well.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.

utterances.text: Now, I'd like to look at some ways you can reduce staff turnover in your hotels, and I'll do this by giving some examples of hotels where I've done some training recently.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: The Sun Club received feedback which showed that staff thought managers didn't value their opinions.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: They weren't made to feel they were partners who were contributing to the success of the business as a whole.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: This situation has changed.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Junior staff at all levels are regularly invited to meetings where their ideas are welcomed.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q15: The Sun Club now invites junior staff to meetings where *'their ideas are welcomed'*. This makes staff feel like valued partners, which improves **relationships and teamwork**. So the answer is **A**.

utterances.text: A year ago, The Portland recognized the need to invest in staff retention.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Their first step was to introduce a scheme for recognizing talent amongst their employees.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q16: The Portland introduced a scheme for *'recognizing talent'* and training those with *'management potential'*. This gives staff a path to grow in the company — that is **providing career opportunities**. The answer is **C**.

utterances.text: The hope is that organizing training for individuals with management potential will encourage them to stay with the business.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: At Bluewater, managers decided to recognize 50 high achievers from across the company's huge hotel chain as a reward.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: They're sent on an all-expenses-paid trip abroad every year.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q17: Bluewater Hotels sends high achievers on an *'all-expenses-paid trip abroad every year'*. A free trip is a reward, which is an **incentive and financial benefit**. The answer is **B**.

utterances.text: Fun is an important element in the trips, but there's also the opportunity to learn something useful.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: This year's trip included a visit to a brewery, where staff learned about the new beer that would be served in the hotel.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Pentlow Hotels identified that retention of junior reception staff was an issue in order to encourage them to see that working in a hotel could be worthwhile and rewarding, with good prospects, they introduced a management program.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q18: Pentlow Hotels introduced a *'management program'* and gave staff *'additional responsibilities'* and *'various roles'*. This shows them a future in the hotel — it is **providing career opportunities**. The answer is **C**.

utterances.text: These staff were given additional responsibilities.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: And the chance to work in various roles in the hotel.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Green Planet wanted to be seen as a caring employer. To make life easier for staff, many of whom had childcare responsibilities,

utterances.text: the hotel began issuing vouchers to help cover the cost of childcare.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Since she joined the company, she's made a huge effort to achieve this.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: By creating a co-operative and supportive environment.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q20: Louise Marsh at the Amesbury created a *'co-operative and supportive environment'* where staff feel like *'family'*. This is all about **improving relationships and teamwork**. The answer is **A**.

utterances.text: For her, the staff are part of a large family where everyone is valued.

audioscript.text: Hello, everyone.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Today we're going to look at another natural food product, and that's maple syrup.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: What is this exactly?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Well, maple syrup looks rather like clear honey, but it's not made by bees.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It's produced from the plant fluid or sap.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Inside the maple tree, and that makes maple syrup a very natural product.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Maple syrup is a thick, golden, sweet-tasting liquid.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says maple syrup is a *'thick, golden, sweet-tasting liquid'* — the question asks for the colour. So the answer is **golden**.

audioscript.text: That can be bought in bottles or jars, and poured onto foods such as waffles and ice cream, or used in the baking of cakes and pastries.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It contains no preservatives or added ingredients, and it provides a healthy alternative to refined sugar.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage says it *'provides a healthy alternative to refined sugar'* — **'alternative'** here means it is a different, better choice. So the answer is **healthy**.

audioscript.text: Let's just talk a bit about the maple tree itself, which is where maple syrup comes from.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So, there are many species of maple tree.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And they'll grow without fertilizer in areas where there's plenty of moisture in the soil.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: However, they'll only do this if another important criterion is fulfilled.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Which is that they must have full or partial sun exposure during the day and very cool nights, and I'll talk more about that in a minute.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: There are only certain parts of the world that provide all these conditions.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: One is Canada, and by that, I mean all parts of Canada.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And the other is the northeastern states of North America.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In these areas, the climate suits the trees perfectly.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says *'the climate suits the trees perfectly'* in Canada and North America — **'climate'** means the weather conditions. So the answer is **climate**.

audioscript.text: In fact, Canada produces over two thirds of the world's maple syrup.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Which is why the five pointed maple leaf is a Canadian symbol, and has featured on the flag since 1964.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So how did maple syrup production begin?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Well, long before Europeans settled in these parts of the world, the indigenous communities had started producing maple sugar.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They bored holes in the trunks of maple trees, and used containers made of tree bark to collect the liquid sap as it poured out.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As they were unable to keep the liquid for any length of time, they didn't have storage facilities in those days.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They boiled the liquid by placing pieces of rock that had become scorching hot from the sun.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says they used *'pieces of rock that had become scorching hot'* to boil the sap — **'scorching hot'** means very hot. So the answer is **rock**.

audioscript.text: Into the sap.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They did this until it turned into sugar, and they were then able to use this to sweeten their food and drinks.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Since that time,
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: improvements have been made to the process, but it has changed very little overall.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So, let's look at the production of maple syrup today.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Clearly, the maple forests are a valuable resource in many Canadian and North American communities.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The trees have to be well looked after, and they cannot be used to make syrup until the trunks reach a diameter of around 25 cm.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says trees cannot be used *'until the trunks reach a diameter of around 25 cm'*, and this *'can take anything up to 40 years'*. So the answer is **diameter**.

audioscript.text: This can take anything up to 40 years.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says trees cannot be used *'until the trunks reach a diameter of around 25 cm'*, and this *'can take anything up to 40 years'*. So the answer is **diameter**.

audioscript.text: As I've already mentioned, maple trees need the right conditions to grow, and also to produce sap.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Why is this?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Well, what happens is that during a cold night, the tree absorbs water from the soil, and that rises through the tree's vascular system.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But then in the warmer daytime, the change in temperature causes the water to be pushed back down to the bottom of the tree.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This continual movement up and down leads to the formation of the sap, needed for maple syrup production.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: When the tree is ready, it can be tapped, and this involves drilling a small hole into the trunk, and inserting a tube into it that ends in a bucket.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage says tapping involves *'inserting a tube into it that ends in a bucket'* — the **tube** carries the sap. So the answer is **tube**.

audioscript.text: The trees can often take several taps, though the workers take care not to cause any damage to the healthy growth of the tree itself.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The sap that comes out of the trees consists of 98% water and 2% sugar and other nutrients.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It has to be boiled, so that much of that water evaporates.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And this process has to take place immediately, using what are called evaporators.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: These are basically extremely large pans.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The sap is poured into these, a fire is built, and the pans are then heated until the sap boils.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says *'a fire is built, and the pans are then heated'* — the **fire** is the means of heating. So the answer is **fire**.

audioscript.text: As it does this, the water evaporates.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And the syrup begins to form.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The evaporation process creates large quantities of steam, and the sap becomes thicker and denser, and at just the right moment, when the sap is thick enough to be called maple syrup, the worker removes it from the heat.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage says the evaporation process *'creates large quantities of steam'* — **'large quantities'** means a lot. So the answer is **steam**.

audioscript.text: After this process, something called sugar sand has to be filtered out, as this builds up during the boiling and gives the syrup a cloudy appearance and a slightly gritty taste.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage says sugar sand *'gives the syrup a cloudy appearance'* — **'appearance'** means how it looks. So the answer is **cloudy**.

audioscript.text: Once this has been done, the syrup is ready to be packaged, so that it can be used for a whole variety of products.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It takes 40 liters of sap to produce 1 liter of maple syrup.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says *'It takes 40 liters of sap to produce 1 liter of maple syrup'* — the question asks for the unit of maple syrup made. So the answer is **litre**.

audioscript.text: So you can get an idea of how much is needed.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So that's the basic process.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
